permalink: articles/ros2_dds_security.html
In ROS 1, this flexibility was valued above all else, at the cost of security.
By virtue of being designed on top of DDS, ROS 2 is able to retain that flexibility while obtaining the ability to be secured by properly utilizing the DDS-Security specification.
This article describes how ROS 2 integrates with DDS-Security.
categories: Security

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview
matches.text: # DDS-Security overview

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview
matches.text: The [DDS-Security specification][dds_security] expands upon the [DDS specification][dds], adding security enhancements by defining a Service Plugin Interface (SPI) architecture, a set of builtin implementations of the SPIs, and the security model enforced by the SPIs.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview
matches.text: - **Authentication**: Verify the identity of a given domain participant.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview
matches.text: - **Access control**: Enforce restrictions on the DDS-related operations that can be performed by an authenticated domain participant.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview
matches.text: - **Cryptographic**: Handle all required encryption, signing, and hashing operations.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview
matches.text: - **Logging**: Provide the ability to audit DDS-Security-related events.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview
matches.text: ROS 2's security features currently utilize only the first three.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview
matches.text: This is due to the fact that neither **Logging** nor **Data Tagging** are required in order to be compliant with the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security] (see section 2.3), and thus not all DDS implementations support them.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Authentication
matches.text: ## Authentication

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Authentication
matches.text: The **Authentication** plugin (see section 8.3 of the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security]) is central to the entire SPI architecture, as it provides the concept of a confirmed identity without which further enforcement would be impossible (e.g. it would be awfully hard to make sure a given ROS identity could only access specific topics if it was impossible to securely determine which identity it was).

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Authentication
matches.text: The SPI architecture allows for a number of potential authentication schemes, but ROS 2 uses the builtin authentication plugin (called "DDS:Auth:PKI-DH", see section 9.3 of the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security]), which uses the proven Public Key Infrastructure (PKI).

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Authentication
matches.text: It requires a public and private key per domain participant, as well as an x.509 certificate that binds the participant's public key to a specific name.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Authentication
matches.text: Each x.509 certificate must be signed by (or have a signature chain to) a specific Certificate Authority (CA) that the plugin is configured to trust.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Authentication
matches.text: 2. It's mandatory for all compliant DDS implementations to interoperably support it (see section 2.3 of the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security]), which makes the ROS 2 security features work across vendors with minimal effort.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Access control
matches.text: The **Access control** plugin (see section 8.4 of the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security]) deals with defining and enforcing restrictions on the DDS-related capabilities of a given domain participant.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Access control
matches.text: Again the SPI architecture allows for some flexibility in how the plugins accomplish this task, but ROS 2 uses the builtin access control plugin (called "DDS:Access:Permission", see section 9.4 of the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security]), which again uses PKI.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Access control
matches.text: - **Governance** file: A signed XML document specifying how the domain should be secured.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Access control
matches.text: - **Permissions** file: A signed XML document containing the permissions of the domain participant, bound to the name of the participant as defined by the authentication plugin (which is done via an x.509 cert, as we just discussed).

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Access control
matches.text: This may be the same CA that the **Authentication** plugin trusts, but that isn't required.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Access control
matches.text: The rationale for using the builtin plugin as opposed to anything else is the same as the **Authentication** plugin:

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Access control
matches.text: 2. It's mandatory for all compliant DDS implementations to interoperably support it (see section 2.3 of the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security]), which makes the ROS 2 security features work across vendors with minimal effort.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Cryptographic
matches.text: The **Cryptographic** plugin (see section 8.5 of the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security]) is where all the cryptography-related operations are handled: encryption, decryption, signing, hashing, etc.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Cryptographic
matches.text: Both the **Authentication** and **Access control** plugins utilize the capabilities of the **Cryptographic** plugin in order to verify signatures, etc.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Cryptographic
matches.text: This is also where the functionality to encrypt DDS topic communication resides.

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Cryptographic
matches.text: While the SPI architecture again allows for a number of possibilities, ROS 2 uses the builtin cryptographic plugin (called "DDS:Crypto:AES-GCM-GMAC", see section 9.5 of the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security]), which provides authenticated encryption using Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois Counter Mode (AES-GCM).

matches.heading: DDS-Security overview / Cryptographic
matches.text: 2. It's mandatory for all compliant DDS implementations to interoperably support it (see section 2.3 of the [DDS-Security spec][dds_security]), which makes the ROS 2 security features work across vendors with minimal effort.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2
matches.text: # DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2
matches.text: Now that we have established some shared understanding of how security is supported in DDS, let's discuss how that support is exposed in ROS 2.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2
matches.text: By default, none of the security features of DDS are enabled in ROS 2.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2
matches.text: The set of features and tools in ROS 2 that are used to enable them are collectively named "Secure ROS 2" (SROS 2).

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL)
matches.text: - Support for security files for each domain participant.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL)
matches.text: - Support for both permissive and strict enforcement of security.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant
matches.text: ### Security files for each domain participant

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant
matches.text: As stated earlier, the DDS-Security plugins require a set of security files (e.g. keys, governance and permissions files, etc.) per domain participant.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant
matches.text: RCL supports being pointed at a directory containing security files in two different ways:

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant
matches.text: - Directory tree of all security files.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Directory tree of all security files
matches.text: #### Directory tree of all security files

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Directory tree of all security files
matches.text: RCL supports finding security files in one directory that is inside the reserved `enclaves` subfolder, within the root keystore, corresponding to the fully-qualified path of every enclave.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Directory tree of all security files
matches.text: - **identity_ca.cert.pem**: The x.509 certificate of the CA trusted by the **Authentication** plugin (the "Identity" CA).

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Directory tree of all security files
matches.text: - **cert.pem**: The x.509 certificate of this enclave instance (signed by the Identity CA).

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Directory tree of all security files
matches.text: - **permissions_ca.cert.pem**: The x.509 certificate of the CA trusted by the **Access control** plugin (the "Permissions" CA).

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Directory tree of all security files
matches.text: - **governance.p7s**: The XML document that specifies to the **Access control** plugin how the domain should be secured  (signed by the Permissions CA).

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Directory tree of all security files
matches.text: - **permissions.p7s**: The XML document that specifies the permissions of this particular enclave instance to the **Access control** plugin (also signed by the Permissions CA).

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Directory tree of all security files
matches.text: This can be specified by setting the `ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE` environment variable to point to the root of the keystore directory tree, and then specifying the enclave path using the `--ros-args` runtime argument `-e`, `--enclave`, e.g.:

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Directory tree of all security files
matches.text: export ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE="/home/bob/.ros/sros2_keystore"

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Manual specification
matches.text: This can be done by setting the `ROS_SECURITY_ENCLAVE_OVERRIDE` environment variable to an alternate enclave path within the keystore.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Manual specification
matches.text: Note that this setting takes precedence over `ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE` with `--enclave`.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Manual specification
matches.text: export ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE="/home/bob/.ros/sros2_keystore"

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Manual specification
matches.text: export ROS_SECURITY_ENCLAVE_OVERRIDE="/front/camera"

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Manual specification
matches.text: export ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE="/home/bob/.ros/sros2_keystore"

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Security files for each domain participant / Manual specification
matches.text: export ROS_SECURITY_ENCLAVE_OVERRIDE="/front/camera"

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Support for both permissive and strict enforcement of security
matches.text: ### Support for both permissive and strict enforcement of security

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Support for both permissive and strict enforcement of security
matches.text: Participants with the security features enabled will not communicate with participants that don't, but what should RCL do if one tries to launch a participant that has no discernable enclave with keys/permissions/etc.? It has two options:

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Support for both permissive and strict enforcement of security
matches.text: - **Permissive mode**: Try to find security files, and if they can't be found, launch the participant without enabling any security features.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Support for both permissive and strict enforcement of security
matches.text: - **Strict mode**: Try to find security files, and if they can't be found, fail to run the participant.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Support for both permissive and strict enforcement of security
matches.text: The type of mode desired can be specified by setting the `ROS_SECURITY_STRATEGY` environment variable to "Enforce" (case-sensitive) for strict mode, and anything else for permissive mode.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Support for a master "on/off" switch for all SROS 2 features
matches.text: In addition to the supported features just discussed, RCL also supports a master shutoff for security features for easy experimentation.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Support for a master "on/off" switch for all SROS 2 features
matches.text: If it's turned off (the default), none of the above security features will be enabled.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the ROS client library (RCL) / Support for a master "on/off" switch for all SROS 2 features
matches.text: In order to enable SROS 2, set the `ROS_SECURITY_ENABLE` environment variable to "true" (case-sensitive).

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the SROS 2 CLI
matches.text: Configuring a ROS 2 system to be secure in RCL involves a lot of new technology (PKI, DDS governance and permissions files and their syntax, etc.).

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the SROS 2 CLI
matches.text: However, the [SROS 2 CLI](https://github.com/ros2/sros2) should include a tool `ros2 security` to help those who don't want to set it all up themselves, including the following capabilities:

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the SROS 2 CLI
matches.text: - Create Identity and Permissions CA.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the SROS 2 CLI
matches.text: - Create directory tree containing all security files.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the SROS 2 CLI
matches.text: - Create a new identity for a given enclave, generating a keypair and signing its x.509 certificate using the Identity CA.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the SROS 2 CLI
matches.text: - Create a governance file that will encrypt all DDS traffic by default.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the SROS 2 CLI
matches.text: - Support specifying enclave permissions [in familiar ROS terms](/articles/ros2_access_control_policies.html) which are then automatically converted into low-level DDS permissions.

matches.heading: DDS-Security integration with ROS 2: SROS 2 / Features in the SROS 2 CLI
matches.text: - Support automatically discovering required permissions from a running ROS system.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }}
matches.text: [SROS 2](/articles/ros2_dds_security.html) introduces several security properties, including encryption, authentication, and authorization.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }}
matches.text: Authorization is obtained by combining the first two properties with a model for access control.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }}
matches.text: A policy serves as a high-level abstraction of privileges associated with attributes that may then be transpiled into low-level permissions for individual identities, such as specific ROS nodes within a secure DDS network.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concepts
matches.text: Before detailing the SROS 2 policy design of the [access control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_access_control), by which the system constrains the ability of a subject to access an object, it is important to establish a few concepts useful in formalizing the design approach in terms of security.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concepts / Mandatory Access Control
matches.text: Most importantly, contrary to discretionary access control (DAC), such policies are enforced by a set of authorization rules that cannot be overridden or modified by the subject either accidentally or intentionally.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concepts / Principle of Least Privilege
matches.text: Applying PoLP not only bolsters system security, but can also ease deployment and help improve system stability.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concepts / Privilege Separation
matches.text: This is used to mitigate the potential damage of a security vulnerability.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concepts / Separation of Concerns
matches.text: Separate concerns in this case may be how encryption is governed in a system versus how authorization is given to subjects.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Criteria / Composition
matches.text: In XML, this is achieved using [XInclude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XInclude); allowing the policy markup to easily include or substitute external reference to particular profiles and permissions that repeat across separate policies or profiles.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Schema / `<metadata>` Tag

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Schema / `<metadata>` Tag
matches.text: This allows advanced users to holistically control the intersect of permissions across transport domains, while retaining accurate model fidelity of security permissions.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Schema / `<metadata>` Tag
matches.text: Given how security sensitive bridge interfaces are and the attack surface they expose, it is vital that information flow control within a bridge remains formally verifiable for safe and secure operation.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Schema / `<metadata>` Tag / Privileges
matches.text: Privileges are defined as configuration of rules and permissions for object access.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Schema / `<metadata>` Tag / Privileges

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Schema / `<metadata>` Tag / Privileges

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Alternatives / YAML
matches.text: Although the policy model used in [SROS 1](http://wiki.ros.org/SROS/Concepts/PolicyDissemination) was semantically equivalent, the YAML format lent it being quite verbose due to repetition of permissions per namespaced resource given the lack of clear element attributes.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Alternatives / Custom
matches.text: As an alternative to choosing an existing markup format, it would be possible to define our own formal language for expressing access control permissions for ROS 2 using a custom file syntax.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Alternatives / Custom
matches.text: Although affording the flexibility to succinctly express profile permission while minimizing general syntactic overhead,  this approach was not pursued for many of the reasons weighed in the following pros and cons:

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Alternatives / ComArmor
matches.text: ComArmor facilitates composition through the use of a nested tree structure of policy/profile/permission primitives.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Alternatives / ComArmor

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Separation of Privileges
matches.text: ROS 2 subsystems such as topics, services, actions, and parameters must eventually map to transport layer interfaces, such as DDS topic, that can sufficiently enforce the desired access control policy in order to secure the ROS application layer.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Separation of Privileges
matches.text: However, any quirks between mapping of subsystems and separation of privileges can degrade security.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Separation of Privileges
matches.text: Such can be exacerbated when using globbing expressions that include matching patterns, such as with `fnmatch`, leading to innocuous and sound policies being inaccurately applied to the underlying transport security.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Separation of Privileges
matches.text: While such privilege separation in [remains week between ROS 2 and DDS](https://github.com/ros2/design/pull/203), perhaps it is wise to discourage the use of expression matching for general use in permissions.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Separation of Concerns
matches.text: Middleware transports, such as DDS, offer a myriad of features and options, such as those for QoS as well as security.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Separation of Concerns
matches.text: Although the SROS 2 policy format was intentionally structured to mimic that of Secure DDS’s permission.xml format, care should be taken when adding extensions to surface non-functional security properties tangential to ROS 2 data flow, such as governance on encryption or discovery.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Composability
matches.text: While it is perhaps unreasonable to expect this dynamic flexibility from staticky provisioned permissions without allocating such capabilities prior, it should be made possible to infer the necessary capabilities from composed launch files and similar orchestrations.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Composability
matches.text: Thus, it stands to reason nodes could instead provide a manifest or IDL defining these nominal requirements so that permission may as easily be remapped, at least at design time.

permalink: articles/ros2_security_enclaves.html
This article specifies the integration of security enclaves.
categories: Security

matches.heading: {{ page.title }}
matches.text: This design document formalizes the integration of ROS 2 with security enclaves.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }}
matches.text: In summary, all secure processes must use an enclave that contains the runtime security artifacts unique to that enclave, yet each process may not necessarily have a unique enclave.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }}
matches.text: Multiple enclaves can be encapsulated in a single security policy to accurately model the information flow control.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concepts / Participant
matches.text: In the case of DDS, the ``Participant`` is a DDS DomainParticipant, which has both access control permissions and a security identity.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concepts / Namespaces
matches.text: Previously, the Fully Qualified Name (FQN) of a node was used directly by a selected security directory lookup strategy to load the necessary key material.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concepts / Namespaces
matches.text: However, now that Participants map to contexts and not nodes, such a direct mapping of node FQN to security artifacts is no longer appropriate.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concepts / Contexts
matches.text: Based on the DDS Security specification v1.1, a ``Participant`` can only utilise a single security identity; consequently the access control permissions applicable to every node mapped to a given context must be consolidated and combined into a single set of security artifacts, or enclave.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Keystore
matches.text: Rather than a flat directory of namespaced node security directories, we can push all such security directories down into a designated `enclaves` sub-folder.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Keystore
matches.text: └── permissions_ca.cert.pem -> ca.cert.pem

matches.text: The ``public`` directory contains anything permissible as public, such as public certificates for the identity or permissions certificate authorities.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Keystore / ``public``

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Keystore / ``enclaves``
matches.text: The ``enclaves`` directory contains the security artifacts associated with individual enclaves, and thus node directories are no longer relevant.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Keystore / ``enclaves``
matches.text: The `ROS_SECURITY_KEYSTORE` environment variable should by convention point to this directory.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Integration
matches.text: With the introduction of contexts into rcl, instead of relying on node namespaces to lookup security artifacts from the keystore, the enclave path is now completely disassociated from node namespaces, instead serving as its own unique resource identifier.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Integration
matches.text: Although having to book keep both identifier spaces simultaneously may introduce more degrees of freedom, it should still be possible to organize enclaves within the keystore to mimic node namespace hierarchy for transparent traceability of allocated permissions.

matches.text: Given the normative case where an enclave within a policy may be specific to a single node/container process, the namespace the node is remapped to will inevitably affect the required security permissions necessary within the enclave.

matches.text: ### Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``
matches.text: Each ``Participant`` subsequently load a security identity and access control credential prevalent to its' respective node.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``
matches.text: There is a mismatch between the middleware credentials/permissions loaded and the resources accessible within the process.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``
matches.text: By using enclaves, all nodes in a context share the same security identity and access control credentials.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``
matches.text: This inevitably means that code compiled to node ``foo`` can access credentials/permissions only trusted to node ``bar``.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``
matches.text: With the introduction of enclaves, it becomes possible to describe the union of access control permission by defining a collection of SROS 2 policy profiles as element within a specific enclave.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``
matches.text: If a process loads a single enclave, this reconciles the permissions of a ``Participant`` and the ones of the process.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``
matches.text: However, should multiple enclaves be loaded per process, then such security guaranties are again lost because of shared same memory space.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``
matches.text: In summary, the distinction here is that before, the composition of multiple node permissions could not be conveyed to the tooling.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Modeling permissions of nodes in a process v.s. permission of the middleware ``Participant``
matches.text: Whether nodes could gain the permission of others in the same process space is not the hinge point of note; it's the fact that such side effects could not be formally modeled or accounted for by the designer.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Composable launchfile includes
matches.text: A particular challenge in using launchfiles with security enclaves is that of keeping the include hierarchy composable.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Composable launchfile includes
matches.text: To be sure though, the setting of security environment variables from within launchfiles should be discouraged, as this would restrict the use of static analysis of launchfiles combined with Node IDL for procedural policy generation.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Composable nodes in container
matches.text: Given that containers can be dynamic, where nodes can be added or removed at runtime, there is perhaps some question as to how containers should integrate with secure enclaves.

matches.heading: {{ page.title }} / Concerns / Migration for RMW implementations
matches.text: For such implementations, the enclave security directory determined by RCL should be loaded for the participant as specified in the "ROS 2 DDS-Security integration" design doc.
